paragraphs.text: The word of God awakens the soul's longing and sets joy around it like a lamp, so that its thoughts may be made bright, its mind made radiant, its sins cleansed and its understanding enlightened. Such is the word of God. What a whetstone is to iron, the word of God is to the soul. A whetstone does not do the iron just one service. First it makes the iron shed its rust. Then it thins the iron when it is thick, sharpens it when it is blunt and brightens it when it is dull: it scours, it polishes, it sharpens. The word of God works the same way. It makes the soul shed the rust of sin, sharpens it when it is blunt, thins it when it is thick and brightens it when it is dark. The word of God wants us to be bright, as the apostle intended when he said, "that you may shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life." There is the brightness. It wants us to be sharp, not blunt: for "the word of God," it says, "is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword." It wants us not to be thick, but to refine our minds with our thoughts. Where there is thickness, there is something foreign to the word of God; where the mind is fine and subtle, there is something akin to the law of God. That is why scripture says of the duller sort: "And Jacob ate and was filled; he grew fat, he grew thick, he grew broad; he forsook God who made him." Come, then, let the divine word shine on our minds too, especially now that this holy fast lies before us, which thins the body and sharpens the mind. For fasting is the nurse of all holiness and the mother of a devout mind. The question is not only how we are to fast, but how we are to fast devoutly. Many people also fast because public business demands it, but it is not counted to them as fasting. The purpose is what is judged; necessity wins no crown. It was in this holy state that blessed Moses was instructed in the law on the mountain and taught about the creation. We told you yesterday that when God was about to give the law through Moses, he first showed himself to be Creator, and only then Lawgiver. How could the Jews have believed that God made heaven and earth and all that is in them, if he had not first worked the wonders in Egypt that showed him to be the Creator of the world? We teach in order to persuade; God persuades in order to teach. Moses was going to set out and declare that God made heaven and earth and sea and all that is in them. If God had not first worked the wonders in Egypt and shown that he is the Creator of all created things, the people would not have believed that God made heaven and earth. So Moses first stretched out his hands toward heaven and brought down hail and fire. Through that faithful servant the peoples learned that if this mortal right hand, moved by the word of God, could shake heaven and throw creation into turmoil, much more did the right hand of God, at his command, set heaven in place and lay the foundations of the earth. For no one can move a creation he did not make. It had to be shown, then, that God made the earth: Moses stretched out his hand over the earth, and gnats came out. Again, it had to be shown that God made fire: Moses took soot from the furnace, scattered it, and covered the bodies of the Egyptians with sores that burned like flame. It had to be shown that God made water: the water was turned into blood. It had to be shown that he made the sea: the sea became solid as rock, and the people passed through. So he first showed by deeds that he is Master, and then explained in words that he is Maker.

In the same way the Savior in the Gospel did not teach until he had worked wonders. His first sign was turning the water into wine, and he does not appear to have taught before that sign. The deed had to come first and the word follow. That is why the writer says: "In my first book, Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach." How was the Savior to teach that he is the Maker of the world? Had he not given light to the eyes of the blind man, he would not have been believed when he said, "I am the light of the world." Had he not raised Lazarus, his hearers would not have believed him when he said, "I am the life and the resurrection." Had he not spat on the ground, made clay and anointed the blind man, no one would have believed that he is the one who took dust from the earth and formed Adam. Had he not walked on the sea, he would not have been seen as Master of the sea. Had he not rebuked the wind, he would not have been shown to be Master of the winds. So he appeared as a man, but through his miracles he was recognized and glorified as God. The Savior astonished his disciples, and they said, "What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?" He first showed the elements obeying him, and then made plain through those deeds that all things came into being through him. He first showed them obeying. Had creation not first been shown to obey, John the evangelist would not have been believed when he said, "All things came into being through him." How could the apostles, with their unlearned speech, have been believed when they bore witness to God the Word, the Creator, the Savior, the all-wise Teacher? Their miracles were their tongue. Their mouth was a dead man raised and a lame man walking. Scripture testifies that faith follows miracles when it says: "Through the hands of the apostles many great signs and wonders were done among the people. All were amazed, and more and more multitudes of men and women were added day by day." The miracles shone out first, and the teachings followed. So it was in the law as well: the wonders in Egypt came first and showed God to be the Creator. But God, being good, did not wish to exalt himself alone, and he shares the glory with Moses. Just as God was revealed by what he made, Moses too is revealed by the glory he was given. When Moses came down holding the law, God filled his face with glory so that they would not treat him as a mere man. In this way the abundance of grace made up what the weakness of nature lacked. They understood that a glorified face is not foreign to God. In the same way the Savior made the face of Stephen the first martyr shine. Why did he make Stephen's face shine? Stephen was going to be stoned as a blasphemer for saying, "I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." So God acted beforehand and crowned his face with the look of an angel, to persuade the unreasonable: if he is a blasphemer, why is he glorified? Yesterday we told you that on the first day God made the things that are out of things that were not. The wonderful thing is that his works not only show that God is the Creator but also refute the impiety of the heretics. For I ask: how did the things that were not come into being, since they ask of him who is, how was he begotten? Let them tell us, if he "was not," how the things that were not came to be when they were not. By human reasoning what is not cannot come into being, though by divine power it can. Sometimes a heretic says, "God spoke, and it came to be." But that states the fact, not the manner. God said, "Let there be light," and what was not came to be. Suppose the word was changed into the thing, as if the voice itself went out and became light. Then it was not made out of things that are not, but out of something that is. For who dares to say that the Word is not? In that case he made nothing out of nothing, but made it out of himself. Then created things turn out to be consubstantial with him, and what they refuse to say of the Son they apply to created things. Hard pressed again, they say, "God's will brought into being the things that were not." So will makes what is not, but nature cannot beget what is? That would be strange indeed! Let me put it in an image. Picture a spring and a rock. Which can more easily produce water, the spring or the rock? If the spring produces water, it brings it out of what it has; the rock brings it out of what it does not have. So the rock produced what was not, out of what it did not have, and the spring could not produce the source it had within itself? And how did the things that were not come into being? Did they happen by chance? Is "what is not" a name, but not something? When I say "out of things that are not," do not suppose that "what is not" is something. So you cannot say how what is came from what is not, and yet you dare to pry into how the One who is was begotten from the One who is? All created things did not exist from the beginning, and then came to be. The only-begotten Word, the Creator of the world, did not come to be from the beginning; he was. These things were not, and then came to be. He was in the beginning without having come to be; they came to be in the beginning, having not been before.

"And the earth was invisible," it says. What does "invisible" mean? I know that many of the holy fathers have said that the earth was invisible because it was covered by water. Many ideas are devout and yet not true. For instance, when Job's three friends saw him in his trial, they condemned the saint as one who was suffering justly. They said, "If you had not grieved widows, if you had not cheated orphans, God would not have brought these things on you." Because they did not know God's purpose, they chose to condemn Job as suffering justly rather than pass judgment on God for afflicting him unjustly. They acted in God's defense, and yet God rebukes them: "Why did you not speak rightly about my servant?" So an idea can be devout and yet not true. What, then, does "and the earth was invisible and unformed" mean? The translators have made it plain. Aquila says, "And the earth was emptiness and nothing." It is called invisible not because it could not be seen, but because it was, so to speak, unadorned. It was not yet made bright with plants, not yet crowned with fruits, not yet girdled with rivers and springs, not yet decked out with the rest of its beauty. It was "invisible" because it had not yet been fitted out to bring forth. Scripture says of a certain brave and handsome man: "Did he not strike down the Egyptian, a visible man?" Is there such a thing as an invisible man? No, it means a man worth seeing. Just as it called the Egyptian a "visible" man because he was worth seeing, so it called the shapeless earth "invisible." On the second day God said: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide water from water." So he made this heaven. He did not make the one above, but the visible heaven, which he congealed out of the waters like ice. I want to set the matter before your eyes, for many things reach us better through sight than through words. Let us say this water stood thirty cubits above the earth. Then God said, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water." A crystal-like solid then set fast in the midst of the waters, lifting half the water up and leaving half below, as it is written: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and it will divide water from water." Why does he call it a firmament? Because he made it firm out of thin, scattered waters. That is why David says, "Praise him in the firmament of his power." To use another illustration: smoke rising from wood and fire is thin and loose, but when it rises high it is reshaped into the thickness of a cloud. In the same way God raised the substance of the thinned waters and made it set solid above. Isaiah bears witness that the illustration is true when he says that heaven was made firm like smoke. So heaven set solid in the midst of the waters and lifted half of them above. But why are there waters above? What use are they? For someone to drink? For someone to sail on? David testifies that there are waters above when he says, "and the water that is above the heavens." Now notice the Creator's wisdom. Heaven was crystalline, congealed from the waters. It was going to receive the flame of the sun and the moon and countless multitudes of stars, and be entirely full of fire. So that the heat would not dissolve or burn it, he spread those seas of water over heaven's back to moisten and anoint it, so that it could withstand the flame and not be scorched. You have an illustration of this too. Even today, if you set a cauldron over a fire, it withstands the fire as long as there is water in it; if there is none, it comes apart. In the same way God set water against fire as its opponent, so that heaven might endure well enough, anointed by the waters above it. And see what a marvel this is. The heavenly body, though assailed by so much fire, has such a surplus of moisture that it even lends some to the earth. Otherwise where does dew come from? There is no cloud anywhere, and the air has no water. Clearly heaven lets it drip down from its surplus. That is why the patriarch Isaac, when he blessed Jacob, said: "May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth."

It is said, brothers, that on the day of judgment the water above will withdraw. Heaven will then dissolve, because the waters no longer hold it together, and the stars will fall, having neither path nor footing. We do not say this idly; scripture teaches it: "For the heaven will be rolled up like a scroll" (that is, as it is scorched, for what is scorched curls up) "and the stars will fall like leaves from a vine." But please notice another use as well. The waters above the heavens not only preserve heaven but also send the flame of the sun and moon downward. If heaven were transparent, all the light would run upward. Fire naturally rises, so it would have left the earth desolate. That is why he covered heaven above with boundless waters: so that the light, hemmed in, would be sent downward. See the Craftsman's wisdom! You also have within yourself an image of the Craftsman's wisdom, for God made an image of the four elements in you as well. Please pay attention. Think of this head of yours as the heaven above, and the part above the tongue as the other heaven, that is, the firmament. That is why it is called the palate, the "little heaven." Above, among the unseen things, is the brain, which is not visible; in the lower part is the tongue, which is visible. In the same way the heaven above belongs to the unseen things, while the world belongs to the things spoken of. Among the elements you find that earth is heavy, and water is lighter than earth but heavier than fire. Again, air is lighter than water but heavier than fire. In the same way our senses, taste, smell, hearing and sight, are not all equal. Here is the proof. If you want to taste something, you get no sensation of it unless you bring it close to your tongue. The tongue is coarse and cannot perceive from a distance. Smell, however, perceives from far away. For example, you pass by a house and smell incense you cannot see. Sight, again, is quicker than smell: from a mountain it sees great expanses. The mind is sharper still than sight. It thinks of heaven, earth and sea, and is found everywhere.

That is why the mind is the image of God. The mind forms a thought, and at once it builds marketplaces within itself and paints a crowd, a whole populace. Let the heretics be ashamed! The mind does such things. Then does not the Craftsman of the mind, who is sharper than any sense of smell, act more swiftly, create more instantly and have a nature beyond comprehension? Brothers, I want to tell you something that is strange in its impiety, though familiar enough to the faith as a matter to examine. Then you will learn how many novelties the devil devises, how many he invents and how many he suggests to the heretics, or rather, how many the heretics suggest to him. Today, in the presence of holy men and fathers, a heretic came to us and spoke. I tell you this so that the story does not reach you in some other form and wound you in some other way. "The Father," he says, "and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one Godhead, one power, one kingdom. But," he says, "we must remove from his soul" (I do not say "from the altar") "the words in the holy hymn: Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth. If you do not take this out," he says, "you are not Christians." Do you see the devil's daring and madness? Do you see the root of the war against God? Do you see how far the blasphemy goes? He wanted to behead piety, cripple the mystery, wipe out the faith and uproot what has been firmly founded. And see the devil's cunning: he planted in the man's mouth the words "Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one faith, one power, one kingdom." He mixed the poison with honey. Whenever a lie wants to be believed, it is not believed unless it first lays a foundation of what looks like truth. Hear how it works. The cases are in no way alike, but I will say it: when Rahab the harlot had taken in the spies, she was asked, "Did the men come to you?" She says, "Yes." The first answer was true. "But they have gone out," she says. The second was a lie. Had she said they had not gone out, the house would have been searched. She told the truth to win their trust, and then added the lie to deceive them. This man did the same. When we asked why we should remove the hymn, he said, "You say 'Lord Sabaoth.' But that is not a name of God, neither of Christ nor of the Father." Do you see that contemptible and foul mouth? In his ignorance he did not know that Sabaoth is not a name of God but a word for armies, so that it means "Lord of hosts." I will also tell you the reason. But before I finish, I bring you good news: he repented, fell down before us, anathematized his error, prayed, and was received.

Pay attention, then. Since the subject has come up, we must also explain why the blessed Isaiah heard this hymn of sanctification being offered up to God. Isaiah was a remarkable man, full of zeal, a bold man, bold not from rashness but from zeal. In those times there was a king named Uzziah, who, on top of all his royal glory, wanted to put on the priesthood as well. The priests knew what the proper order was, but they were unwilling to oppose the king to the end. They respected his rank, they honored his throne, they were overawed by his armies. Isaiah too kept silent and did not stand up to the king. When God saw the priests afraid, the prophet giving way and the king acting with presumption, he struck the king with leprosy on his face for daring to touch the holy things. So from then on he was cast out not only from the priesthood but from the kingship too, and he remained a leper. God had done his part, but he was angry with the priests, and above all with the prophet, because he had been present and had betrayed true religion. So God kept silent toward the prophet and did not share his words with him until the lawbreaker died. When at last the ungodly man was dead, God laid aside his anger and was reconciled to the prophet. So Isaiah says: "And it came to pass in the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up." And why did God appear on a throne high and lifted up? Because God is invisible, while the king, who could be seen, had inspired fear, God shows the prophet the heavenly glory to convince him what kind of throne they had despised and what kind of throne they had honored instead: how they had neither honored nor even thought of a heavenly and angelic bodyguard, and yet had been overawed by a human one. "And the house," he says, "was full of his glory, and the seraphim stood around him." The cherubim are a throne, the seraphim a bodyguard. For "cherubim" means nothing other than "fullness of wisdom." And just as this throne here, or any other, gives rest to the one who sits on it and is both an honor and a resting place, so God's throne is wisdom, on which God rests. That is why David says, "You who sit upon the cherubim," that is, "you who rest upon the fullness of wisdom." That is why the cherubim are full of eyes: their backs, their heads, their wings, their feet, their breasts. Everything was full of eyes, because wisdom sees on every side and keeps its eye open in every direction. "Six wings," he says, "to the one, and six wings to the other. With two they covered their face and with two their feet, and with two they flew. And they cried out one to another: Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth," that is, Lord of hosts. Six wings to the one and six wings to the other: eight are still and four cry out. What, then, does Scripture teach us? Not to set every thought in motion about God, but to proclaim some things by silence, and to glorify others by faith and speak of them as theology. And why do they cover their feet and their head? Because neither a beginning nor an end is to be found. With two they cover the head, with two the feet; clearly, then, they fly with the middle wings, not the upper ones and not the lower ones. For when we speak about God we must speak of the middle things: that he is God, that he is Creator, that he is Master, that he is Benefactor. All these are middle things. If you ask how he begot, you have uncovered the head that the cherubim cover. If you ask where God's end is, you uncover the feet that the cherubim cover. They cover the head and the feet not to hide them but to teach that these things cannot be searched out and cannot be comprehended. Take the figure too. There were six and six, twelve wings; eight are still and four are in motion. It is a figure of the apostles: twelve apostles, but four evangelists cry out. And what do they cry? The very cry that Satan has been eager to overturn. Pay attention, I beg you. They did not simply say, as we do, "Holy, holy, holy"; rather, one answered the other, as it is written: "And they cried out one to another." "Holy," it says: we should say it once. The other says, "Holy." Then the next one, add the third: "Holy." Now since we have counted three, do not think there are three gods. Why then "Holy, holy, holy Lord"? Because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism. And just as in the singing of psalms the parts answer one another, so the powers above dance in answer to one another and send up their doxology as if in antiphonal song. Then: "The house," he says, "was full of his glory. And the lintel was lifted up at the sound of the cry with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke."

A strange thing! After the doxology, when glory ought to have been added, even the glory that was there vanished and smoke came in. And smoke is an image of desolation. What, then, does this mean? The Holy Spirit foresaw that the "Holy, holy, holy" was suited to the world, to the preaching of the apostles, and that the temple of the Jews would not receive it. So he is saying that after the preaching of the gospel the synagogue is filled with desolation and smoke. And it was not the door that was lifted up but the lintel. Pay attention. Every door has a threshold underneath it and a lintel lying on top of the doorposts. Doorposts cannot stand without a threshold, nor can they be held firm and unshaken without receiving the lintel. So what was lifted up was the upper structure of the synagogue. Not the whole synagogue: it still has doors, but it has no lintel. The lintel is the power that holds it together from above. "The lintel was lifted up": it was stripped of grace. Once the lintel has been lifted up, the doorposts are bound to be shaken by any hand that comes along. That is why every hand shakes the things of the Jews. And that is why a prophet said, "And I will make Jerusalem like a doorway that is shaken." "And the house," he says, "was filled with smoke." And where did the glory go? Pay attention, I beg you. Isaiah says, "And his house was full of glory." Then he says that it was filled with smoke. When the smoke came in, then, the glory must have moved elsewhere. And where did it move? Not into a single house: it filled the churches throughout the whole inhabited world. And to show where the glory that was in the temple had gone, the cherubim say, "The whole earth is full of his glory." One nation was stripped bare, and the ends of the earth were filled with light. This holy cry of the Lord, this royal doxology, this divinely inspired initiation into the mysteries, a devilish mouth was saying: "Remove it from the altar." That the blasphemy is aimed at Christ himself, the testimony makes clear. Whom did Isaiah see on the throne? For he says, "I heard the voice of the Lord saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" He had been reconciled to his servant, but he still bore something of his anger. Just as when we are reconciled with a servant we do not at once grant him our full gaze but gently steal glances at him, so God, not wishing to show his whole face, says while the prophet stands there, "Whom shall I send?" It is as when servants stand before their master and he wants to rebuke their laziness, and says, "Whom shall I send? I have no one for this job," not meaning that he has no one, but that he has no one diligent. So too God: "Whom shall I send in place of this man? The one who kept silent? The one who fought against the priesthood?" What, then, does Isaiah do? Like a servant who has given offense, stung and eager to make amends for what went before: "Here am I; send me." How then can we show that the glory was Christ's? John the Evangelist says: "Though Jesus had done such signs, the Jews did not believe in him, so that the word spoken through Isaiah might be fulfilled: Hearing you will hear, and will not understand. Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke about him." Do you see that the hymn of sanctification is the very heart of our salvation? Unless the sanctification takes place, the mystery is not performed either. You have the image. No sooner had the cherubim said, "Holy, holy, holy Lord," than the sacrifice was sanctified. "And one of the cherubim," he says, "was sent to me, and in his hand he held a coal, which he had taken with the tongs from the altar." He did not take it until it had been sanctified. "He touched my lips," he says. Why the lips? They are the doorway of the mysteries. What do we the faithful say? That this mystery forgives sins. And the cherubim say too, "Behold, I have taken away your sins." Do you see the figure? Do you see the truth shining forth? Let us, then, never cease to hallow him who sits on the throne high and lifted up. And let us also give thanks for the soul that was lured away, which the wolf seized and the shepherd tore back, which the devil snatched and the Lover of mankind took away from him, so that every heretical mouth and every tongue that raves blasphemy may hymn the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to the ages. Amen.
